topics.title: EQ Presets — headphone corrections from OPRA
topics.body:
This thread is for headphone corrections and presets.
What it's for: starting from a measurement instead of from scratch. 6,229 headphones and 12,594 published curves ship offline from OPRA, the community directory of headphone EQ profiles, grouped by brand and credited to whoever measured them — oratory1990, the AutoEq project, Rtings.
How it works: a published correction is applied as a layer of its own, beside your bands, with its own strength and switch — so clearing your EQ does not throw it away. For anything not in OPRA, Squiglink works as a guided import: export the EQ text there, paste it here, preview the curve, and it becomes editable bands. A whole output's tuning exports as a .fluideq file and imports back onto the output you are listening to.
The library can update on its own, and every release carries the current database with it.
Ask here about corrections for your model, Squiglink imports, and sharing chains.

Renamed and rewritten for 1.4: this tab was AutoEQ, and the data was AutoEq's. OPRA replaced it — the tab is EQ Presets now.

topics.title: Voicing — the thirteen target curves
topics.body:
This thread is for the Voicing tab.
What it's for: a starting point by taste. Thirteen curated target curves — music, movies, games, speech and late night, plus rock, metal, pop, hip-hop and R&B, electronic, jazz, classical and acoustic.
How it works: a voicing is written into the chain after your bands, so it never overwrites your own tuning — switch it off and your EQ is exactly as you left it. Each curve has a strength slider, and the decibel changes it makes are spelled out on its card rather than hidden.
Ask here about which curve fits what, and what a voicing is actually doing to the sound.

topics.title: Config — what Equalizer APO actually has on disk
topics.body:
This thread is for the Config tab.
What it's for: seeing what Equalizer APO actually has on disk — not what FluidEQ intends. The two differ exactly when it matters: after a hand edit, another tool, or a restore from backup.
How it works: every layer is a file of its own, included per output, and the tab shows that include tree as it really is — what each file holds, which layers are on, and any include pointing at nothing. Each output also gets one file FluidEQ creates and never rewrites, applied last, for the APO commands that have no interface here; its filters are drawn on the graph and counted in the preamp. From here a whole chain exports to a .fluideq file and imports back.
Ask here about the config layout, hand edits, and moving chains between machines.

topics.title: Karaoke Maker — building the file when the song has none
topics.body:
This thread is for the Karaoke Maker.
What it's for: making the karaoke file when the song does not have one.
How it works: open a song and it walks the whole way. The words can be transcribed from the audio or pasted in and kept. Transcription downloads a speech-recognition model the first time you use it — on your press, never at launch. It is the one thing in FluidEQ that reaches the network for something other than an update, and pasting the words in skips it entirely. Timing is recorded by ear — mark each line as the track plays, then individual words where a line needs the detail. The melody is read off the recording into notes you can hear, split, retune, delete or add to by hand. Undo and redo run throughout, Restore original rebuilds the import, and the result goes straight to the player or saves as a project.
Ask here about transcription, timing, the melody editor and project files.

topics.title: Karaoke — singing over your own files
topics.body:
This thread is for the Karaoke tab.
What it's for: singing over files you already own. Audio can be MP3, WAV, OGG, FLAC or M4A; lyrics can be .lrc for line timing, enhanced .lrc for word timing, or an UltraStar .txt for syllables and real target notes.
How it works: the words follow the audio's own clock, so a long song cannot drift away from them. Your microphone is chosen and switched on by you, analysed on your own machine, never recorded and never played back through the speakers. The pitch lane draws target notes only when the file genuinely carries them, the chord guide is estimated from the backing track and says so, and a review collects the bars you drifted on and counts you back in.
What it does not do, by design: it does not remove vocals, separate stems, or change key or tempo — the instrumental is something you bring.
Ask here about formats, the pitch lane, chords and the stage.

topics.title: Media — the built-in player
topics.body:
This thread is for the Media tab.
What it's for: something to tune against. A player inside FluidEQ — YouTube, YouTube Music, Bandcamp, Twitch and Suno — with the response graph and live spectrum moving underneath it.
How it works: it goes to those sites and nowhere else; it is not a browser. You can sign in and it remembers you next time — its cookies live in a store of their own that no other part of FluidEQ reads, and one button in its toolbar throws the whole lot away. Google sign-in may refuse inside an embedded view; that one is not ours to fix.
Ask here about the player, sign-ins, and a site behaving oddly inside it.

topics.title: Convolution — impulse responses
topics.body:
This thread is for the Convolution tab.
What it's for: applying a measured impulse response ahead of everything else — verified minimum-phase responses from the AutoEq catalogue, or any WAV of your own.
How it works: the file is analysed when it arrives, so the graph draws the response the file actually has rather than an approximation published beside it, and the preamp reserves against what it really does. It is a layer with its own switch, so hearing the chain without it is one press.
Ask here about impulse responses, importing your own WAVs, and what convolution is for in the first place.

topics.title: EQ — bands, filter types and the preamp
topics.body:
This thread is for the EQ tab — your own bands.
What it's for: the tuning you place by hand. Up to 128 bands per output, and every filter type Equalizer APO understands — peak, low shelf, high shelf, low pass, high pass, band pass and notch — each with frequency, gain and Q.
How it works: your bands are one layer in the chain, with a switch of their own. The driver correction, headphone correction, voicing and Smart EQ are separate layers, so clearing your bands never touches them. Every layer feeds a single computed preamp: Auto normalize reserves headroom against the real combined response, so stacking layers cannot clip you, and removing one gives the volume back.
Ask here about bands, filter types, the preamp and Auto normalize. If the sound is wrong rather than the question, that is a bug — the issue tracker is the better place, so it does not get lost.

topics.title: FluidEQ community
topics.body:
I'm Ivan, and I wrote FluidEQ. This is the place for questions, for anything behaving oddly, and for things you'd like it to do.
Worth knowing before you ask:

FluidEQ is a graphical interface for Equalizer APO. Windows only, and APO ships inside the installer — you don't have to go and find it.
It's GPL-3.0. The source is in this repository, and the build on the Releases page is free. Windows will warn about the publisher, because that build isn't code-signed yet.
If something is genuinely broken rather than just confusing, the issue tracker is a better place than this thread — it doesn't get lost.

I'm one person, so an answer might take a day. It will be me answering, not a support queue.
